passage: In the corridors of their Mumbai school, everyone knew the map: the football boys by the water cooler, the debate kids near the library, the backbenchers on the stairs. Chinmay, fifteen, belonged to the football boys. When he was paired with Ganga from the debate kids for the history project, his friends groaned. "Library people? Good luck, bro." At lunch he had to pick: his usual spot by the cooler, or the library table where Ganga was waiting with a plan. He stood in the corridor longer than he meant to. Then he went to the library. When his friends passed and whistled, his ears went red. But Ganga's plan was actually good, and by the end of the period he'd forgotten the whistling.

qa.q: Where did the football boys hang out?
qa.a: By the water cooler.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay stand in the corridor longer than he meant to?
qa.a: He was torn between staying with his group and going to work with Ganga, knowing that crossing over might bring teasing.

qa.q: How could Chinmay handle his friends' whistling next time?
qa.a: Shrug it off with a light reply or explain it's a project, so the line feels less rigid without a fight.

qa.q: How might Ganga have experienced waiting at the library table?
qa.a: She might have wondered whether he would show up at all, given which group he belongs to.

grounding: It shows a teenager navigating the strict lines between school groups when a project crosses them.

passage:
"You're not sitting with us anymore?" Saurabh asked.
Francis shifted his tray. "The band guys asked me. We're planning the fest."
"So you're a band guy now."
"I play guitar, Saurabh. I've always played guitar."
"You never sat with them before."
"They never asked before." Francis sighed. "Why does it have to be one table or the other?"
"Because that's how it works here. You pick."
"Then I pick both. Monday and Wednesday with you. Tuesday and Thursday with them."
Saurabh snorted. "They'll never let you do that."
"Watch me."
But on Tuesday, when Francis sat with the band, one of them said, "Your cricket friends coming too?" and nobody laughed.

qa.q: Which days did Francis offer to sit with Saurabh?
qa.a: Monday and Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling when he said "So you're a band guy now"?
qa.a: Hurt and a little jealous, worried that Francis was leaving his group behind.

qa.q: What could Francis do if the band members keep making remarks?
qa.a: Answer calmly that he is friends with both, and perhaps invite Saurabh to a practice to bridge the groups.

qa.q: What does the band member's remark on Tuesday suggest about how they see groups?
qa.a: They also see people as belonging to one group, which is why the idea of two tables meets suspicion.

grounding: It shows a teenager trying to cross strict group boundaries and meeting resistance from both sides.

passage: In Class 10, our group had rules nobody said out loud. You wore the same kind of hair clips. You didn't sit with the hostel kids. You laughed at the same people. When Wasim, who'd been with us since Class 6, started sitting with the hostel boys for chess, the group froze him out. No invites, no replies in the chat. I went along with it for about a week. Then one day I saw him eating alone on the steps, and I felt sick. I sat down next to him. "Gurleen?" he said, surprised. The next morning my group had moved seats. It hurt. But looking back, that was the day I understood how tight those lines were, and that I didn't want to live inside them.

qa.q: Why did Wasim start sitting with the hostel boys?
qa.a: To play chess.

qa.q: What did Gurleen feel when she saw Wasim eating alone?
qa.a: Sick and guilty about having gone along with freezing him out.

qa.q: What could Gurleen have done to make the move feel less lonely?
qa.a: Find one or two others who felt the same, or talk to a trusted adult, so as not to face the group alone.

qa.q: How might Wasim have seen Gurleen sitting down next to him?
qa.a: Surprised and relieved, since Gurleen was the first from the group to cross the line back to him.

grounding: It shows a teenager recognising and stepping outside a clique's rigid rules about who belongs.

passage: Coach's note, inter-house practice, week three. Class 9 has split into two lunch groups, and it shows on the field: the 'front-row' group passes only to each other. Today Noor, who sits with that group, was put on a team with Manoj and two others from the other side. For ten minutes she hung back. Then Manoj saw her open and passed; she scored and he whooped. Afterwards I saw her glance toward her usual friends before walking off with her new teammates for water. One of her friends said something to her and she shrugged, face tight. Next step: I will mix teams by drawing lots every week, so no one has to cross over alone, and I'll keep an eye on how Noor is doing at lunch.

qa.q: How will teams be picked from next week?
qa.a: By drawing lots every week.

qa.q: What does Noor's glance toward her usual friends suggest she was worried about?
qa.a: She may have worried her friends would see walking off with the new teammates as leaving their group.

qa.q: Why might drawing lots help?
qa.a: It takes the choice out of students' hands, so mixing is not seen as betraying anyone's group.

qa.q: How might Manoj have seen Noor after the goal?
qa.a: His whoop suggests he was glad to include her and saw her as a real teammate.

grounding: Shows how rigid group lines at school affect a teenager who crosses them, noticed by a coach.

passage: Friday. So Pema has been at school three weeks and still eats alone. He's actually funny; I found out in the chemistry lab when he gave all our test tubes names. Today I asked the guys if he could sit with us, and it went weird. Nobody said no. They just said 'he's not really our type' and changed the topic. What is our type? We're five boys who play the same game and wear the same shoes. I didn't push it. I hate that I didn't. Maybe on Monday I'll just go sit at his table instead. They can't kick me out of a table I leave. Or they can make it awkward forever. I'll decide on Monday. – Dhruv

qa.q: How long has Pema been at the school?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: What does 'I hate that I didn't' show about Dhruv's feelings?
qa.a: He felt ashamed that he let the group's quiet refusal stand, even though he likes Pema.

qa.q: What small step could Dhruv try on Monday?
qa.a: He could sit with Pema for one lunch, or bring one friend along, to show that group lines can be crossed.

qa.q: What is lunchtime likely like for Pema right now?
qa.a: Probably lonely, eating alone while the groups around him have already formed.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager running into his group's unspoken rule about who belongs and weighing whether to cross it.

passage: At the small-town school, the popular group always sat under the neem tree. Aadhya, fifteen, had been part of it since Class 8. Abhinav, from the science club, was her neighbour and her oldest friend. One day he walked over to ask about the bus. Before Aadhya could answer, a girl in her group said, "We don't really mix, na?" Abhinav's face went still. Aadhya felt every eye on her. She stood up. "I'll walk with you to the gate," she said to him. Later, the group was cool with her for a week. She decided that was a price she could pay.

qa.q: Where did the popular group sit?
qa.a: Under the neem tree.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when every eye was on her?
qa.a: She felt pressured and torn between her group and her old friend.

qa.q: What did Aadhya's choice achieve, and at what cost?
qa.a: It kept her friendship with Abhinav, but cost her a week of coldness from the group.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have felt when the girl said "We don't really mix"?
qa.a: Embarrassed and hurt, as if he'd been shut out of Aadhya's world.

grounding: Shows a teenager testing the strict boundaries of her social group to stay loyal to an old friend.

passage: On her first day at a high school in Toronto, Layla, sixteen, stood with her tray in the cafeteria doorway. The map was clear within seconds: the athletes by the windows, the theatre kids near the stage, the gamers at the back. Every table had its own invisible fence. Aiko, from her maths class, waved her over to the theatre table. Layla sat. Someone asked, "Do you act?" "No," Layla said. The table went a bit quieter. "But I paint sets," she added. Aiko grinned. "Then you're ours." Layla smiled, but she noticed how quickly the question had come.

qa.q: What did Layla say she does?
qa.a: She paints sets.

qa.q: What might Layla have felt when the table went quieter?
qa.a: She was probably nervous and unsure, sensing she might not belong.

qa.q: What would you advise Layla as she settles in?
qa.a: Keep being honest about her interests and get to know people across tables, not just one group.

qa.q: How does Aiko see Layla joining the table?
qa.a: Aiko is welcoming and happy to find a reason to include her.

grounding: Shows a teenager noticing the strict boundaries between social groups on her first day at a new school.

passage: In the Kanpur school canteen, the tables had rules nobody had written. The toppers sat by the window. The sports boys took the long table. Everyone else filled the gaps. Sunaina, a topper, was paired for the science project with Chetan, the cricket captain. On Monday he walked over with his tray. The toppers went quiet. Sunaina felt their eyes and shifted her bag onto the empty chair without thinking. Chetan paused. Then she moved the bag back. "Sit. We need to plan." Her friend Pooja raised an eyebrow. At the long table, the sports boys were whistling. Sunaina kept her face calm, but her hands were cold around her glass. Chetan pulled out his notebook as if nothing had happened.

qa.q: Where did the toppers sit?
qa.a: By the window.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling as her hands went cold around her glass?
qa.a: She felt anxious and self-conscious, aware of both groups watching her break the unwritten rule.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Moving the bag back so Chetan could sit, because the project mattered more than the table rules.

qa.q: How might Chetan have felt when Sunaina first put her bag on the chair?
qa.a: He may have felt unwelcome and awkward, before being invited to sit.

grounding: A teenager crosses an unwritten canteen boundary to sit with a project partner from another group.

I'm Ujjwal, I sit two benches behind Nilesh in Class 10. Since the start of term, the back-row lot, the cricket boys, have owned the corner near the window. Nilesh isn't one of them. He's in the quiz crowd.
Last week the cricket boys needed a scorer for the inter-class match and one of them waved Nilesh over. He went, and for three days he ate lunch with them. I saw his quiz friends watching from across the room.
On Friday one of the cricketers laughed at something Nilesh said about a quiz. Nilesh laughed too, but then he picked up his tiffin and went back to his old bench.
I can't tell if he was hurt or just tired of pretending. He sat very straight, and the quiz boys made room without a word.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have been feeling when he went back to his old bench?
qa.a: He may have felt hurt or tired of pretending, and perhaps relieved to be back where he was accepted.

qa.a: A teacher could mix groups for projects so students work across the lines without making anyone feel singled out.

passage:
Day one: Sunaina joined St. Anne's in Class 11. By lunch she understood the map: the science toppers by the lab, the dance girls by the stage, the hostellers at the far table. Nobody said the rules. Everyone knew them.
Two weeks later: Vishal, from the hosteller table, needed a partner for chemistry. She agreed. The dance girls stopped saving her seat. One of them said, too sweetly, "Oh, you're with them now?" Sunaina felt her face burn and said nothing.
A month in: She sat with Vishal's group on Mondays and with the dance girls on Thursdays, and when someone commented, she shrugged. "I eat where my friends are." Some of them still didn't like it. She decided she could live with that.

qa.q: Where did the hostellers sit?
qa.a: At the far table.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel when the dance girl said "Oh, you're with them now?"
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and stung; her face burned and she said nothing.

qa.q: What would you advise Sunaina if the comments kept coming?
qa.a: Keep calmly eating with the friends she chooses and, if it turns into bullying, talk to a teacher or counsellor.

qa.q: How might Vishal see Sunaina sitting with his group?
qa.a: Vishal may feel pleased and a little surprised that someone from outside the hostel crowd chose to sit with them.

grounding: Shows a new student learning and then quietly crossing unspoken group boundaries over several weeks.

Lakshmi, beta, you say your school has groups that won't mix. Let me tell you about my college hostel in Pune, long ago.
There were the Marathi boys, the Bengali boys, the rich boys with scooters. I, Lalit, was from a small town and fit nowhere. For the first term I ate alone and pretended to read.
Then one evening the Bengali boys needed someone for their carrom team. I was good at carrom. I played. The next day the Marathi boys teased me for switching sides. I nearly stopped playing.
But I kept going to both corridors. I played carrom with one group and cricket with the other. It took a year, but by the end some of them came to my room together.
So choose people, Lakshmi, not corners.

passage: The school trip bus to Jaipur was leaving in five minutes, and Kashish still hadn't picked a seat. The back rows belonged to Tanya's group; everyone knew that without being told. Tanya called, "Kash, we saved you one!" The teacher shouted, "Sit anywhere, now!" Kashish felt both groups watching. She sat with Kunal, then turned and said to Tanya, "Swap at the lunch stop?" Tanya shrugged, lips tight. Kunal handed her an earphone. "Quiz on the way?"
